lectures.label: Lecture 37
lectures.title: Nitrogen Balance, Protein Digestion and Transaminases

slides.note: Correction: glutamate is made from α-ketoglutarate (α-KG, a citric acid cycle intermediate) by adding an amino group, not the reverse. Also, the ~30 g/day in the figure is what leaves the pool to build nitrogen-containing compounds (heme, creatine, neurotransmitters, purines, pyrimidines); the amount of non-essential amino acids made varies. The amino acid pool (~90–100 g of free amino acids in cells and blood) is filled by the three sources on top and emptied by the uses below.

Negative: more nitrogen leaves than comes in, because body protein is broken down faster than it is rebuilt (too little intake, or the catabolic stress of fever, burns or wasting disease). Positive: the body is building new tissue and keeps nitrogen. After starvation the body rebuilds the protein it lost, so the balance turns positive.

a.a. = amino acid. Endopeptidases cut bonds inside the chain; exopeptidases clip one amino acid off an end (aminopeptidase from the N-terminus, carboxypeptidase from the C-terminus). Zymogens are inactive precursors that switch on only after a piece is cut off, so the pancreas does not digest itself. Pepsinogen is activated by HCl and by pepsin itself. Free amino acids and di- and tripeptides are absorbed and reach the liver through the portal vein.

Correction: only trypsin, chymotrypsin and elastase are serine proteases; carboxypeptidases A and B are zinc-dependent exopeptidases. Follow the blue arrows: enteropeptidase (also called enterokinase) on the brush border cuts trypsinogen into trypsin. Trypsin then activates more trypsinogen and all the other zymogens, so one trigger starts the whole cascade.

Each enzyme cuts the bond right after certain residues. Trypsin: basic Arg, Lys. Chymotrypsin: bulky aromatic Phe, Trp, Tyr (plus Met, Leu). Elastase: small Ala, Gly, Ser. Carboxypeptidase removes the last amino acid at the C-terminus: A takes neutral ones (Ala, Ile, Leu, Val), B takes basic ones (Arg, Lys).
Correction: “serine proteases” covers trypsin, chymotrypsin and elastase only. Carboxypeptidase is a zinc enzyme, not a serine protease.

Cystine is two cysteines joined by a disulfide bond. Of the four lost amino acids it is the only one too insoluble to stay dissolved, so only cystine forms stones; ornithine, arginine and lysine just wash out. The same carrier works in the gut. Lab: hexagonal crystals in the urine. Treatment: plenty of fluids and alkaline urine.

The faulty carrier moves neutral (uncharged) amino acids, so they are lost in stool and urine. Losing Trp (tryptophan) is what causes disease, because the body makes part of its niacin (vitamin B3, used to build NAD⁺) from Trp. Low niacin gives pellagra: sun-sensitive dermatitis, diarrhea and dementia or ataxia. Nicotinic acid is niacin, so supplements fix it.

Correction: CFTR is a chloride (Cl⁻) channel; water follows Cl⁻ out of cells. Without it, secretions dry into thick mucus that plugs the pancreatic ducts, so pancreatic enzymes cannot reach the gut. Fat and protein go undigested, giving steatorrhea (bulky, greasy, foul stools). Lab: high sweat Cl⁻. Treatment: pancreatic enzyme pills with meals.

Gliadin (the harmful part of gluten, found in wheat, barley and rye) triggers an immune attack on the small-intestine lining. The villi flatten (villous atrophy), so the absorbing surface shrinks. Lab: IgA antibodies against tissue transglutaminase. The MHC link is HLA-DQ2/DQ8 (HLA = the human MHC genes).

ALT and AST normally sit inside cells. When cells die, the enzymes leak into blood, so high serum levels mean cell damage. Liver holds most of the body's ALT, so ALT is the more liver-specific marker (think ALT = Liver). AST also leaks from damaged heart and skeletal muscle. IU/L = international units of enzyme activity per liter.

Blue line: ALT leaks from injured liver cells within hours and peaks at ~20× normal around 1.5 days, so it is an early marker. Orange line: bilirubin rises only after ~36 h, once so much liver is lost that it can no longer conjugate and excrete bilirubin. Bilirubin then builds up and causes jaundice (yellow skin and eyes).

Transamination: only the amino group (red) moves. Alanine becomes its keto acid, pyruvate, and α-KG becomes glutamate. Each carbon skeleton keeps its size (3C stays 3C, 5C stays 5C). The reaction runs both ways. SGPT is ALT's old name.

Aspartate gives its amino group to α-KG, making oxaloacetate (OAA) and glutamate. SGOT is AST's old name. The asterisk: during amino acid breakdown AST mostly runs in reverse. Glutamate hands its amino group to OAA, and the aspartate formed carries the second nitrogen into the urea cycle.

Follow the red boxes. In muscle, amino groups from broken-down protein collect on glutamate, and ALT moves them onto pyruvate, making alanine. Alanine carries the nitrogen through blood to the liver in a non-toxic form. In liver, ALT runs backward: alanine becomes pyruvate again, and glutamate releases NH₃ through glutamate dehydrogenase (Glu DH); the NH₃ is turned into urea. Pyruvate is made into glucose, which returns to muscle.

PLP (pyridoxal phosphate, the active form of vitamin B6) is the cofactor of every aminotransferase. It carries the amino group for a moment, in two steps. Top: glutamate hands its NH₂ (red box) to PLP and becomes α-KG, while PLP becomes pyridoxamine phosphate. Bottom: pyridoxamine phosphate passes the NH₂ to oxaloacetate, making aspartate, and turns back into PLP.
Answer: C. Saliva has no protease. Protein digestion starts in the stomach with pepsin, continues with pancreatic enzymes and ends with peptidases on the small-intestine brush border.

Answer: C. Enteropeptidase on the brush border makes the first trypsin, and trypsin activates the rest. Trypsinogen and chymotrypsinogen are inactive zymogens, pepsinogen belongs to the stomach, and carboxypeptidase activates nothing.

Answer: A. Hartnup blocks uptake of Trp, which the body uses to make niacin; niacin deficiency is pellagra. Cystinuria loses only cystine, ornithine, arginine and lysine, so it causes stones, not pellagra.

Answer: D. ALT leaks from injured liver cells and is the most liver-specific enzyme on the list. Enterokinase (another name for enteropeptidase), pepsin and trypsin are gut digestive enzymes; PLP is a vitamin cofactor, not a marker of injury.

High NH₃ drains the brain's fuel. It pushes α-KG (α-ketoglutarate) into glutamate (Glu) and Glu into glutamine (Gln). That pulls α-KG and OAA (oxaloacetate) out of the TCA (citric acid) cycle, so ATP falls. Astrocytes store NH₃ as Gln, but Gln enters their mitochondria, where mitochondrial glutaminase frees the NH₃ again. This makes ROS (reactive oxygen species), damages the mitochondria and swells the astrocytes, causing brain edema.

Blood NH₃ comes mostly from the gut (about half; colon bacteria break down urea and protein) and the kidney (about 40%; it splits glutamine). The kidney sends much of its NH₃ into urine as NH₄⁺ (ammonium), which carries acid out of the body.

ALT (alanine aminotransferase) and AST (aspartate aminotransferase) move the amino group (pink) from an amino acid onto α-KG, making glutamate. They need PLP (pyridoxal phosphate, the active form of vitamin B6) and release no free NH₃. Glutamate dehydrogenase then strips the amino group off glutamate as NH₄⁺ (circled) and gives back α-KG.

Top arrows (NAD⁺): glutamate → α-KG + NH₃. This is the liver direction after a protein meal; the NH₃ goes to urea and the α-KG to the TCA cycle. Bottom arrows (NADPH): the reverse, which traps NH₃ in glutamate only when NH₃ is high, as in the brain. The concentrations of the reactants decide the direction.

Glutamine synthetase (uses ATP) adds NH₃ to glutamate in muscle, brain and other tissues, making glutamine to carry NH₃ safely in blood. Glutaminase (mainly liver, kidney, gut) frees the NH₃ again: the liver turns it into urea, and the kidney excretes it as NH₄⁺. Synthetase traps NH₃; glutaminase releases it.

Many tumors burn glutamine. Glutaminase frees one NH₃ (Gln → Glu), glutamate dehydrogenase (Glu DH) frees a second (Glu → α-KG), and α-KG enters the TCA cycle through α-KGDH (α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase) to make ATP. Breast cancer cells recycle the NH₃: Glu DH runs backward to make glutamate, which supplies N for new amino acids.
Periportal hepatocytes are the liver cells closest to where portal blood from the gut enters each lobule, so they meet the incoming NH₃ first.

Both urea N atoms come from glutamate: glutamate dehydrogenase frees one as NH₃ (used to make carbamoyl phosphate), and AST moves the other onto oxaloacetate to make aspartate. The carbon comes from CO₂. '4 ATP' means 4 high-energy bonds: 3 ATP are used, but one is split to AMP + PPi (pyrophosphate), which costs 2 bonds. Steps 1–2 run in mitochondria, steps 3–5 in cytosol.

CPS I (carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I) is the rate-limiting step. It works only when NAG (N-acetylglutamate) binds it as an allosteric activator. Don't confuse it with CPS II, which sits in the cytosol, takes N from glutamine, needs no NAG, and starts pyrimidine synthesis.

OTC (ornithine transcarbamoylase) moves the carbamoyl group, carrying the first N, onto ornithine to make citrulline; the phosphate leaves as Pi (free phosphate). 'No codon' means ornithine and citrulline are never built into proteins. A transporter swaps citrulline out of the mitochondrion for ornithine coming in.

ASS (argininosuccinate synthetase) joins citrulline to aspartate. Aspartate's amino group becomes urea's second N. AST supplies the aspartate by moving glutamate's amino group onto OAA. Splitting ATP to AMP + PPi spends 2 high-energy bonds; this is the cycle's third and last ATP.

ASL (argininosuccinate lyase) splits argininosuccinate: the N stays on arginine, and aspartate's carbon skeleton leaves as fumarate. Follow the blue arrows: fumarate → malate → OAA (by MDHc, cytosolic malate dehydrogenase) → aspartate (by AST), which feeds step 3 again. Malate can instead enter mitochondria for the TCA cycle. This links the urea and TCA cycles.
The kidney has ASS and ASL, so it turns citrulline made by the gut into arginine. It cannot make urea, because only the liver splits arginine into urea with arginase.

The whole cycle. Shaded right side = mitochondrial matrix (1 CPS1, 2 OTC); left = cytosol (3 ASS, 4 ASL, 5 arginase). Follow the pink N atoms: one enters as free NH₃ at step 1, the other comes from aspartate at step 3. The green C comes from CO₂. All three end up in urea (red box), and ornithine goes back into the mitochondrion to start the next turn.

In the figure, about 75% of urea leaves in urine (blue line). About 25% diffuses into the colon (red line), where bacterial urease splits it into NH₃, and the portal vein (green line) carries that NH₃ back to the liver. In kidney failure, blood urea rises, more of it reaches the gut, and the extra NH₃ raises blood ammonia. (“Renal aorta” on the slide means the renal artery.)

BUN rises when the kidneys filter less (kidney disease, dehydration) or when the liver makes more urea from extra amino acids (high-protein diet, tissue breakdown, blood digested after a GI bleed, glucocorticoids breaking down muscle). It falls when the liver makes less urea (liver disease) or less protein comes in.

Short term (feed-forward): more amino acids → more glutamate and arginine → more NAG → faster CPS I. Long term: a high-protein diet and fasting both raise the amount of every urea-cycle enzyme. In fasting, glucagon boosts gluconeogenesis from amino acids: alanine from muscle becomes pyruvate in the liver, and its amino group must leave as urea.

Any block stops urea, so NH₃ rises and the body parks the excess as glutamine (Gln) and alanine (Ala). The cycle makes arginine, so arginine falls, except in arginase deficiency, where it piles up. Tell the defects apart by what builds up before the block. OTC: unused carbamoyl phosphate (CP) leaks to the cytosol, where ATCase (aspartate transcarbamoylase, pyrimidine pathway) turns it into orotic acid. CPS1: no CP, so no orotic acid. ASS: citrulline. ASL: argininosuccinate.

Normal plasma NH₃ is under about 35 µM. NH₃ stimulates the brain's breathing center, so the baby breathes fast and blows off CO₂, causing respiratory alkalosis. The edema comes from glutamine swelling astrocytes. Partial defects stay silent until protein breakdown rises (illness, fasting, stress) and overwhelms the weak cycle.

Phenylbutyrate becomes phenylacetate, which joins glutamine; the product (phenylacetylglutamine) leaves in urine and carries 2 N out without the urea cycle. Citrulline (CPS1 or OTC deficiency) enters the cycle after the block and picks up aspartate's N. Arginine (ASS deficiency = citrullinemia; ASL deficiency = ASA, argininosuccinic aciduria) replaces the arginine the cycle can't make, regenerates ornithine and activates NAG synthase.
Answer: D. AST and ALT only transfer the amino group to α-KG to make glutamate; no free NH₃ is released. MAO, glutamate dehydrogenase, glutaminase and adenosine deaminase all release free NH₃.

Answer: D (OTC deficiency). High NH₃ + low BUN = urea is not being made; fast breathing = NH₃-driven respiratory alkalosis. Orotic acid points to OTC: carbamoyl phosphate is made but can't enter the cycle, so it spills into pyrimidine synthesis. CPS1 deficiency looks the same but has no orotic acid, because no carbamoyl phosphate is made.

Every amino acid splits into two parts. The amino group (red circle) comes off and leaves the body as urea. The carbon skeleton (blue box, now an α-keto acid) is burned for energy or becomes glucose or ketone bodies, depending on which molecule it turns into. TCA = tricarboxylic acid (Krebs) cycle.

Rule: a skeleton that becomes pyruvate or a TCA intermediate (red boxes) can make glucose, because all of these lead to oxaloacetate → phosphoenolpyruvate → glucose. A skeleton that becomes acetyl CoA or acetoacetate (blue box) can only make ketone bodies, because acetyl CoA cannot be turned back into pyruvate. Leucine and lysine give only acetyl CoA/acetoacetate. The three aromatic amino acids (Phe, Tyr, Trp) plus isoleucine give both.

DHAP = dihydroxyacetone phosphate. In fasting, muscle protein breaks down and alanine carries its carbons to the liver, where it becomes pyruvate → glucose. Don't confuse: fatty acids normally cannot make glucose; only the last 3 carbons of an odd-chain fatty acid (propionyl CoA) can.

Conditionally essential = normally made, but the supply can fall short. Tyrosine needs enough phenylalanine (and a working phenylalanine hydroxylase); cysteine needs enough methionine. Arginine is made via ornithine and the urea cycle, but not fast enough for a growing child.

Synthesis of non-essential amino acids mostly runs these breakdown steps in reverse. Transamination is reversible, so oxaloacetate → aspartate. Asparagine is made by asparagine synthetase (aspartate + an amide N from glutamine, using ATP). Asparaginase treats ALL (acute lymphoblastic leukemia) because the leukemic cells lack asparagine synthetase (red X), so they starve once the drug destroys blood asparagine.

Glutaminase removes glutamine's amide NH₂ as NH₃, leaving glutamate. Glutamate → α-KG (α-ketoglutarate) two ways: transamination (hands its amino group to a keto acid) or glutamate dehydrogenase (releases free NH₃). Reversed, these build glutamate; glutamine is built by glutamine synthetase (glutamate + NH₃ + ATP). PLP (pyridoxal phosphate, the active form of vitamin B6) is the cofactor of every aminotransferase.

Both lines are routes into α-KG. Arginine → ornithine (arginase) → glutamate semialdehyde → glutamate → α-KG; proline is also oxidized to glutamate. For synthesis, run it backward: glutamate → glutamate semialdehyde → proline, or → ornithine → urea cycle → arginine. So proline and arginine share one precursor. The kidney finishes arginine (from citrulline made in the gut) and keeps it, because it lacks the liver's urea-cycle arginase.

Serine hydroxymethyltransferase (PLP) moves one carbon between glycine and serine: glycine + a carbon from N⁵,N¹⁰-methylene-THF (tetrahydrofolate, the active folate) → serine; the reverse makes glycine. Serine itself is mainly made from 3-phosphoglycerate, a glycolysis intermediate. Serine dehydratase turns serine into pyruvate. In humans, threonine goes mainly to succinyl CoA (via propionyl CoA).

Answer: D. Arginine is made from glutamate via ornithine, but a growing child cannot make enough (conditionally essential). Tryptophan, threonine and phenylalanine are essential, so they cannot be made at all; serine is made freely from 3-phosphoglycerate.

BH₄ (tetrahydrobiopterin) is the cofactor of the three aromatic amino acid hydroxylases: Phe → Tyr, Tyr → DOPA (first step to catecholamines), Trp → 5-hydroxytryptophan (first step to serotonin). Nitric oxide synthase (Arg → NO) also needs it. Each reaction oxidizes BH₄ to BH₂ (dihydrobiopterin); dihydropteridine reductase rebuilds BH₄. The body makes BH₄ from GTP, so it is not a vitamin.

Missing dihydropteridine reductase (the ‘BH₂ reductase’) or a BH₄-making enzyme leaves no BH₄. Phe then builds up, as in PKU (phenylketonuria), and dopamine, norepinephrine and serotonin fall. That transmitter loss causes the neurologic signs, so a low-Phe diet alone does not fix it. Treat with BH₄ (sapropterin) plus L-DOPA and 5-hydroxytryptophan.

Read the left column downward: the one carbon on THF gets more reduced at each step: formyl (–CHO) → methenyl (=CH–) → methylene (–CH₂–) → methyl (–CH₃). Each form has its job (blue boxes): N¹⁰-formyl → purines; N⁵,N¹⁰-methylene → dTMP (deoxythymidine monophosphate, the T of DNA) and serine; N⁵-methyl → methionine. MTHFR = methylene-THF reductase. The neural tube closes about 4 weeks after conception, often before pregnancy is known, so folate must be adequate beforehand.

Histidine breaks down via FIGLU (N-formiminoglutamate). The last step hands FIGLU's one-carbon group to THF, leaving glutamate → α-KG. With folate deficiency there is no THF to take it, so FIGLU builds up and spills into urine, especially after a histidine load (the FIGLU test). Histidinemia is a different defect: missing histidase, the first step, so histidine itself rises in blood and urine.

Follow the arrow down. Met + ATP → SAM (S-adenosylmethionine). SAM gives its methyl to an acceptor → SAH (S-adenosylhomocysteine) → homocysteine. Homocysteine has two exits. Remethylation back to Met (methionine synthase) needs N⁵-methyl-THF (folate) and methyl-B12. Transsulfuration needs vitamin B6: homocysteine + serine → cystathionine → cysteine + α-ketobutyrate (→ succinyl CoA). So low folate, B12 or B6 raises homocysteine, a vascular risk factor; missing cystathionine β-synthase causes homocystinuria.

All five feed propionyl CoA (mnemonic VOMIT, in slide order: Val, Odd-chain fatty acids, Met, Ile, Thr). Propionyl CoA carboxylase (needs biotin) → methylmalonyl CoA; methylmalonyl CoA mutase (needs B12) → succinyl CoA → glucose. Low B12 blocks the mutase, so methylmalonic acid rises; this separates B12 deficiency from folate deficiency.

Each target receives SAM's methyl group; SAM then becomes SAH → homocysteine, which is recycled to methionine. Polyamines are the exception: they take SAM's aminopropyl part, not its methyl. Methylation is needed to build and keep myelin, so poor methylation (e.g., low B12) can cause demyelination.

Tyrosine hydroxylase (BH₄) is the rate-limiting step. Dopamine β-oxidase is the same enzyme as dopamine β-hydroxylase (needs copper and vitamin C). The last step, NE → epinephrine, is PNMT (phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase), using a methyl from SAM. Cortisol from the adrenal cortex induces PNMT, so epinephrine is made mainly in the adrenal medulla. Side branch: in melanocytes, tyrosinase (a copper enzyme) makes melanin; no tyrosinase = albinism.

Two enzymes inactivate catecholamines, in either order: MAO (monoamine oxidase) removes the amine; COMT (catechol-O-methyltransferase) adds a methyl from SAM. Dopamine ends as HVA (homovanillic acid). Epinephrine and norepinephrine pass through metanephrines and end as VMA (vanillylmandelic acid). A pheochromocytoma (adrenal medulla tumor making catecholamines) raises urine VMA and metanephrines.

Niacin (vitamin B3, used to build NAD⁺): too little causes pellagra, with dermatitis (the neck rash pictured), diarrhea and dementia. Melatonin is made from serotonin in the pineal gland and regulates sleep. Hartnup disease: the gut and kidney transporter for neutral amino acids is defective, so tryptophan is poorly absorbed and lost in urine → too little niacin → pellagra-like rash and neurologic signs.

Trp → 5-hydroxytryptophan (tryptophan hydroxylase, BH₄) → serotonin (decarboxylase, PLP). Left arrows: a carcinoid tumor makes lots of serotonin, MAO turns it into 5-HIAA (5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid), so urine 5-HIAA rises (the diagnostic test). An MAO inhibitor blocks that step: serotonin stays high and 5-HIAA falls. SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) raise synaptic serotonin by blocking its reuptake into the neuron.

Removing the amino group leaves an α-keto acid (the carbon skeleton). Removing the carboxyl group as CO₂ (decarboxylation, needs PLP) leaves a biogenic amine, such as histamine, serotonin, dopamine or GABA.

Both are single decarboxylations that need PLP (vitamin B6). Histamine acts on H1 receptors (allergy, inflammation; blocked by antihistamines) and on stomach H2 receptors (acid secretion; blocked by H2-blocker acid reducers). Glutamate decarboxylase turns the brain's main excitatory transmitter into its main inhibitory one, GABA (γ-aminobutyric acid).

Glutathione (G-SH; Glu-Cys-Gly) is the cell's main antioxidant. Glutathione peroxidase (a selenium enzyme) uses 2 G-SH to turn H₂O₂ into water, leaving G-S-S-G; glutathione reductase rebuilds G-SH with NADPH from the pentose phosphate pathway. The lower-left picture is heme, not bile acid: glycine + succinyl CoA → ALA (δ-aminolevulinic acid) by ALA synthase (PLP), the rate-limiting step. Lower right: bile acids are conjugated to glycine or taurine.

Creatine needs two organs. The kidney moves arginine's amidino group onto glycine → guanidinoacetate; the liver adds a methyl from SAM → creatine. Muscle stores it as creatine phosphate, a quick ATP reserve for the first minutes of hard exercise. Creatine slowly and spontaneously cyclizes into creatinine at a steady rate set by muscle mass. Creatinine is cleared by filtration, so blood creatinine rises when GFR (glomerular filtration rate) falls.

lectures.label: Lecture 40
lectures.title: Inborn Errors of Amino Acid Metabolism

slides.note: Phe becomes Tyr by PAH (phenylalanine hydroxylase), which needs O₂ and BH₄. In the reaction BH₄ turns into BH₂, which is recycled back to BH₄ with NADH. Each red bar marks a disease: a block at PAH or at BH₄ recycling causes PKU, at Tyr → melanin causes albinism, and in Tyr breakdown causes tyrosinemia. When PAH is blocked, Phe spills into the side products at upper left (phenylpyruvate, phenylacetate, phenyllactate), which harm the brain.

Non-classical PKU comes from failure to make or recycle BH₄ (e.g. dihydropteridine reductase deficiency, the lower X). BH₄ is also the cofactor of tyrosine hydroxylase and tryptophan hydroxylase, so these patients also lack dopamine, norepinephrine and serotonin. A low-Phe diet alone does not fix their brain symptoms; they also need BH₄, L-DOPA and 5-hydroxytryptophan.

With PAH blocked, Phe takes a minor route. An aminotransferase moves its amino group onto pyruvate (making alanine), using PLP (pyridoxal phosphate, the active form of vitamin B6). The product, phenylpyruvate, is a phenyl-ketone. It spills into the urine, gives the disease its name and a musty, “mousy” odor, and is turned into phenylacetate and phenyllactate.

Blood Phe rises 20–50-fold. Phe shares one brain-entry transporter with the other large neutral amino acids (Tyr, Trp, Val, Leu, Ile) and wins the competition, so the brain runs short of them for protein, myelin and neurotransmitters. That is why treatment adds back Tyr, Trp and the branched-chain amino acids while restricting Phe. In PKU, Tyr becomes an essential amino acid.
Answer: D. Classical PKU is a deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase. Dihydropteridine reductase (A) deficiency causes the non-classical, BH₄-type PKU.

Read down the pathway; each disease (yellow) sits beside its blocked enzyme. THB = BH₄ (tetrahydrobiopterin) and DHB = BH₂ (dihydrobiopterin); dihydrobiopterin reductase is the same enzyme as dihydropteridine reductase. Nitisinone is a drug that blocks p-hydroxyphenylpyruvate oxidase. Ochronosis is the black pigment that alkaptonuria deposits in cartilage.

HT1 is a deficiency of fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase, the last step. Fumarylacetoacetate and maleylacetoacetate back up and form succinylacetone, which damages the liver and the kidney tubules (glucose, phosphate and amino acids leak into urine) and blocks heme synthesis. Succinylacetone in blood or urine is the diagnostic marker. Nitisinone blocks an earlier step so these toxins never form; Tyr then rises, so the low-Phe/Tyr diet is still needed.

Both blocks sit before fumarylacetoacetate, so no succinylacetone forms and the liver is spared; instead tyrosine itself builds up. In HT2 (oculocutaneous tyrosinemia) Tyr is very high and forms crystals in the cornea and skin, causing the photophobia and painful palm/sole lesions. HT3 hits the same enzyme that nitisinone blocks.

Don't confuse tyrosinase (copper enzyme in melanocytes, no BH₄; Tyr → DOPA → melanin) with tyrosine hydroxylase (BH₄ enzyme in neurons and adrenal medulla; Tyr → DOPA → catecholamines). Without melanin the iris lets light through (red-looking eyes, photophobia) and the skin has no UV shield (skin cancer).
Answer: E. Succinylacetone forms from the backed-up fumarylacetoacetate (B) and maleylacetoacetate (D). It is the toxic product that damages liver and kidney, and the marker used to diagnose HT1.

Each branched-chain amino acid (BCAA: Val, Ile, Leu) first hands its amino group to α-ketoglutarate; then BCKD removes the carboxyl as CO₂ and adds CoA. BCKD works like PDH (pyruvate dehydrogenase) and α-KGDH (α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase) and shares their E3 subunit. Its cofactors come from vitamins: TPP (thiamine pyrophosphate) from B1, FAD from B2, NAD⁺ from B3, CoA from B5, plus lipoic acid. This happens mainly in muscle, not liver.

Propionyl-CoA → methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA. The last step needs methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and its B12 form, adenosyl-cobalamin. Type I breaks either the enzyme (mut⁰ = no activity, mut⁻ = low) or the making of adenosyl-cobalamin (cblA, cblB). Methylmalonic acid builds up and causes acidosis. Backed-up propionyl-CoA blocks NAG (N-acetylglutamate) synthetase; without NAG, CPS-I (carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I, the first urea-cycle enzyme) stays off, so ammonia rises. Homocysteine stays normal.

Answer: D. Thiamine becomes TPP, the cofactor of BCKD's E1 subunit; extra TPP can rescue a mutant E1 that binds it weakly. PDH, α-KGDH and transketolase also use TPP, but none of them is defective in MSUD. Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase uses B12.

Follow homocysteine (Hcy); it has two exits. (1) Back to methionine by methionine synthase, which needs methyl-cobalamin (B12) and takes the methyl from 5-methyl-TH₄ (TH₄ = tetrahydrofolate, active folate). (2) On to cysteine by cystathionine β-synthase, then cystathionase; both need PLP (B6). Top loop: methionine + ATP makes SAM (S-adenosylmethionine), which gives its methyl to X and becomes S-adenosylhomocysteine, then Hcy. Low B6, B12 or folate lets Hcy build up.

Classic homocystinuria is cystathionine β-synthase deficiency: Hcy and methionine rise, and cysteine falls (it becomes essential). B12 or folate deficiency instead raises Hcy with normal or low methionine. The lens dislocates downward (in Marfan syndrome it goes upward), and blood clots are the main cause of early death. Some patients respond to large doses of B6.

cblC, cblD and cblF are early processing steps (Cblₓ = cobalamin on its way to an active form) shared by both B12 forms. So both B12 enzymes fail: methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (needs adenosyl-cobalamin) and methionine synthase (needs methyl-cobalamin). Labs show high methylmalonic acid and high homocysteine, the same pattern as dietary B12 deficiency. Folate deficiency raises homocysteine only.
Answer: C. Hcy inhibits lysyl oxidase, the copper enzyme that cross-links collagen fibers. Weakly cross-linked collagen makes a poor bone matrix, so bone mineral density falls.

SAM (S-adenosylmethionine) donates methyl groups; PAPS (3′-phosphoadenosine-5′-phosphosulfate) donates sulfate groups. UDP-glucose (uridine diphosphate-glucose) builds glycogen, and CDP-linked head groups (cytidine diphosphate) build phospholipids. Each of these carriers contains a nucleotide.

The ring is built step by step on PRPP (5-phosphoribosyl-1-pyrophosphate, the activated form of ribose 5-phosphate). The yellow numbers give the order in which atoms are added. Atoms per donor: glycine 3 (2 C + 1 N), glutamine 2 N, N¹⁰-formyl-THF 2 C, aspartate 1 N, CO₂ 1 C. THF = tetrahydrofolate, the form of folate that carries one-carbon units.

PRPP (phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate, an activated ribose) gets its first nitrogen from glutamine in the committed step, glutamine:PRPP amidotransferase. AMP, IMP and GMP feed back to inhibit that step (the ⊖). Nine more steps build the ring on the sugar to make IMP (inosine monophosphate; base = hypoxanthine). IMP then branches: N from aspartate gives AMP; IMP dehydrogenase plus N from glutamine gives GMP.

This step commits PRPP to purines, because 5-phosphoribosylamine has no other use. (PRPP synthetase is not committed: PRPP also feeds pyrimidine synthesis and salvage.) The end products AMP, GMP and IMP inhibit it; PRPP activates it. The drugs 6-mercaptopurine and allopurinol are turned into nucleotides by HGPRT (hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase, a salvage enzyme), and those nucleotides also block this step.

Dotted lines are feedback. Each product blocks the first enzyme of its own branch: AMP blocks adenylosuccinate synthetase, GMP blocks IMP dehydrogenase. The crossing solid lines show the balance: making AMP uses GTP, and making GMP uses ATP, so a surplus of one purine drives production of the other. When both are plentiful, they also shut off the amidotransferase and PRPP synthetase.

Mycophenolic acid blocks IMP dehydrogenase (IMP → XMP → GMP). B and T lymphocytes depend on de novo purine synthesis because they salvage poorly, so they run short of GMP and dGTP (deoxyguanosine triphosphate, a DNA building block) and cannot multiply. Most other cells keep going on salvage, so the drug mainly suppresses the immune attack on a transplant.
Answer: C, glycine. It donates 3 ring atoms (2 C + 1 N), more than any other source.

Phosphoribosylation = moving the ribose 5-phosphate from PRPP onto a free base, which releases pyrophosphate (PPi). Breakdown of the PPi makes the reaction irreversible. HGPRT salvages hypoxanthine (→ IMP) and guanine (→ GMP); APRT (adenine phosphoribosyltransferase) salvages adenine (→ AMP). Salvage matters most in the brain.

Severity follows how much HGPRT activity is left: almost none → Lesch-Nyhan (neurologic signs, self-biting); partial → Kelley-Seegmiller (gout and uric acid kidney stones, no self-injury). In APRT deficiency, adenine cannot be salvaged and is oxidized to 2,8-dihydroxyadenine, which is insoluble and forms kidney stones (renal lithiasis).

Why uric acid rises: hypoxanthine and guanine that cannot be salvaged are broken down to uric acid. Also, the PRPP that HGPRT would have used builds up, while IMP and GMP fall. The amidotransferase gets more activator and less inhibition, so de novo synthesis speeds up and makes still more purine to degrade → hyperuricemia, gout and uric acid kidney stones. X-linked recessive, so it affects boys.
Answer: A. HGPRT attaches guanine (and hypoxanthine) to PRPP. B, C and D are de novo steps and E is PRPP synthetase; all of these still work, and de novo synthesis actually speeds up.

CPS II (carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II) makes carbamoyl phosphate from glutamine's amide N, CO₂ and 2 ATP. ATCase (aspartate transcarbamoylase) then adds aspartate, and the closed ring is attached to PRPP. UMP (uridine monophosphate) comes first; UTP (uridine triphosphate) → CTP (cytidine triphosphate) feeds RNA. The DNA thymine nucleotide, dTMP, is made from dUMP (deoxyuridine monophosphate), not directly from UTP.

Follow the steps:
1. CPS II: glutamine + CO₂ + 2 ATP → carbamoyl phosphate (the regulated step).
2. ATCase adds aspartate → carbamoyl aspartate.
3. Dihydroorotase closes the ring → dihydroorotate.
4. Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (inner mitochondrial membrane) oxidizes it → orotate.
5. Orotate phosphoribosyltransferase adds ribose-P from PRPP → OMP (orotidine monophosphate).
6. OMP decarboxylase removes CO₂ → UMP.

Steps 1–3 are one protein, CAD; steps 5–6 are one protein, UMP synthase.
Answer: A, aspartate (4 atoms: 3 C + 1 N). Glycine and N¹⁰-formyl-THF give none, because they donate only to purines.

Pyrimidine salvage goes through nucleosides: a phosphorylase adds the sugar (from ribose 1-phosphate) to the base, then a kinase adds the phosphate. Purine salvage is different: HGPRT and APRT attach ribose-phosphate from PRPP directly. Salvaged uridine bypasses the de novo pathway, which is why uridine treats orotic aciduria.

Orotate cannot be turned into UMP, so it builds up and spills into the urine. Without pyrimidine nucleotides, fast-dividing marrow cells cannot copy DNA → megaloblastic anemia that does not improve with vitamin B12 or folate, plus leukopenia. Uridine is salvaged straight to UMP, past the block; the UTP made from it also turns CPS II back down.

Follow the dashed line: with OTC (ornithine transcarbamoylase) blocked, carbamoyl phosphate made by CPS I in mitochondria leaks into the cytosol. It enters the pyrimidine path after CPS II, so UTP feedback cannot stop it, and orotate is made faster than UMP synthase can use it. Ammonia rises because the urea cycle is blocked, but pyrimidine supply stays normal, so there is no anemia.

N-glycosidic bond = the bond that joins the base to the sugar. Purines make it first (ring built on PRPP); pyrimidines make it last. In humans the regulated, rate-limiting step of pyrimidine synthesis is CPS II (inhibited by UTP); ATCase is the regulated step only in bacteria. The one mitochondrial enzyme is dihydroorotate dehydrogenase.
Answer: B. UTP inhibits CPS II, the enzyme that produces carbamoyl phosphate. The others: A = PRPP synthetase, C = orotate phosphoribosyltransferase, D = dihydroorotate dehydrogenase, E = ATCase.

Ribonucleotide reductase removes the 2′-OH from the ribose of ADP, GDP, CDP and UDP (one enzyme for all four). The hydrogens come from NADPH, passed through thioredoxin (recycled by thioredoxin reductase). dATP (deoxyadenosine triphosphate) turns the whole enzyme off and ATP turns it on, so too much dATP halts DNA synthesis. Hydroxyurea blocks this enzyme and starves dividing cells of DNA building blocks.

Follow the loop: thymidylate synthase uses N⁵,N¹⁰-methylene-THF to add a methyl to dUMP → dTMP, which leaves DHF (dihydrofolate). DHFR (dihydrofolate reductase, uses NADPH) turns DHF back into THF. Methotrexate blocks DHFR, so THF runs out → no dTMP and no purines (which need N¹⁰-formyl-THF). 5-FU (5-fluorouracil), as its nucleotide 5-FdUMP (fluoro-dUMP), blocks thymidylate synthase itself.

Selectivity: humans don't make folate, so sulfonamides (which block folate synthesis) hit only microbes. Trimethoprim binds bacterial DHFR, and pyrimethamine binds protozoal DHFR, far more tightly than human DHFR. Methotrexate blocks human DHFR, so it is an anticancer drug. Bacteriostatic = stops growth without killing.
Compare the two ring structures: sulfanilamide looks like PABA (p-aminobenzoic acid, a building block of folate), so it competes with PABA at dihydropteroate synthetase.
Methotrexate looks almost like folate (NH₂ instead of OH at C4, a methyl on N10), so it binds DHFR very tightly. DHFR does both reductions shown (folate → DHF → THF), so both are blocked.

Normally thymidylate synthase grips dUMP through an enzyme cysteine (–SH), links it to methylene-THF, then pulls off the hydrogen at C5 to release dTMP. In 5-FdUMP, fluorine sits where that hydrogen must leave and cannot be removed, so enzyme, drug and folate stay locked in a stable covalent adduct. Suicide inhibitor = the enzyme's own reaction traps it.

All three are inactive until cells turn them into nucleotides. 6-MP (6-mercaptopurine) is activated by HGPRT; its nucleotide blocks IMP → AMP/GMP and the amidotransferase. 5-FU becomes F-UTP (built into RNA) and F-dUMP (blocks thymidylate synthase). AraC (cytosine arabinoside) carries arabinose instead of ribose; as araCTP it blocks DNA polymerase.

Both drugs must be phosphorylated to nucleotides before they work. Neither has a 3′-OH, so once built into DNA, no next nucleotide can attach (chain termination). The herpes virus's own thymidine kinase does the first phosphorylation of acyclovir, so the active drug forms mainly in infected cells. Correction: AZT is 3′-azido-3′-deoxythymidine, not 2′.
Answer: B, pyrimethamine. It blocks the DHFR of protozoa. Sulfonamides and trimethoprim target bacteria; methotrexate and 5-FU target human cells (anticancer).
Correction: AZT (zidovudine) is 3′-azido-3′-deoxythymidine, not 2′-azido. The azido group replaces the 3′-OH, which is why it stops DNA chain growth. Acycloguanosine = acyclovir.

Every purine nucleotide follows the same steps: nucleotide → nucleoside (5′-nucleotidase removes the phosphate) → free base (PNP, purine nucleoside phosphorylase, removes the ribose) → xanthine → uric acid. Adenine first loses its amino group (AMP → IMP by AMP deaminase, or adenosine → inosine by ADA, adenosine deaminase), so it ends up as hypoxanthine. Guanine is deaminated to xanthine by guanase. IMP = inosine monophosphate (base: hypoxanthine); XMP = xanthosine monophosphate.

Xanthine oxidase does the last two steps: hypoxanthine → xanthine → uric acid. Each step uses O₂ and releases H₂O₂ (hydrogen peroxide). Its key metal cofactor is molybdenum; FAD (flavin adenine dinucleotide) and Fe-S (iron-sulfur) centers carry the electrons. Tissues outside the liver and gut have little of it, so their free bases are kept for salvage.

Answer: A. Xanthine oxidase oxidizes hypoxanthine → xanthine, then xanthine → uric acid. D (inosine → hypoxanthine) is PNP's reaction, E (adenosine → inosine) is ADA's, C skips the xanthine step, and B runs backward.

HGPRT (hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase) and APRT (adenine phosphoribosyltransferase) reattach free bases to ribose phosphate, remaking IMP, GMP and AMP. This salvage pathway rescues about 90% of bases. The green and purple boxes mark the two bases HGPRT rescues. Without HGPRT, hypoxanthine and guanine can only go to xanthine oxidase, so uric acid rises.

PRPP (5-phosphoribosyl-1-pyrophosphate) is the activated ribose-phosphate donor for both salvage and new (de novo) purine synthesis. Salvage uses up PRPP and makes AMP, IMP and GMP, which inhibit glutamine:PRPP amidotransferase, the committed step of de novo synthesis. So active salvage slows de novo synthesis; lost salvage (Lesch-Nyhan) speeds it up.

Underexcretion causes over 90% of hyperuricemia. Lactate raises urate because the kidney's URAT1 (urate transporter 1) takes urate back from the tubular fluid in exchange for lactate — more lactate, more urate reabsorbed. Chemotherapy kills many cells at once and releases their purines, so uric acid spikes.

Under polarized light, gout crystals (MSU, monosodium urate) are needles, negatively birefringent (yellow when parallel to the compensator axis). Pseudogout crystals (calcium pyrophosphate) are rhomboid, positively birefringent (blue when parallel). Tophi = chalky lumps of urate crystals in soft tissue; podagra = a gout attack in the big-toe (first metatarsophalangeal) joint.

HGPRT is almost absent, so hypoxanthine and guanine are not salvaged and become uric acid. Unused PRPP piles up and IMP/GMP fall, so de novo synthesis speeds up — a second source of urate. Orange "sand" in the diaper = uric acid crystals. Neurological signs include chorea and athetosis (jerky and writhing involuntary movements). Allopurinol lowers urate but does not fix the neurological or self-injury symptoms.

• von Gierke (glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency): glucose 6-phosphate builds up and spills into the HMP shunt (hexose monophosphate shunt = pentose phosphate pathway) → more ribose 5-phosphate → more PRPP → more purines made and degraded. It also causes lactic acidosis.
  • Hereditary fructose intolerance (aldolase B deficiency): fructose 1-phosphate traps phosphate, ATP can't be regenerated, and the extra AMP is broken down to urate.
  • Alcohol raises lactate, which blocks urate excretion.

Answer: D. More PRPP drives more de novo purine synthesis, and the extra purines are degraded to uric acid. B (more salvage), C (less xanthine oxidation, like allopurinol) and E (less AMP breakdown) all lower uric acid. A involves pyrimidines, which never become uric acid.

Each treatment targets one source. (2) A low-purine diet cuts intake (diet supplies about one-third of purines). (3) Xanthine oxidase inhibitors cut production in overproducers. (4) Uricosuric drugs raise kidney excretion in underexcretors (reduced renal clearance, blue X, is the most common cause). (1) NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs), colchicine and steroids only calm the acute flare; they do not lower uric acid.

Colchicine binds tubulin and blocks microtubule assembly, so neutrophils cannot move into the joint or engulf crystals. NSAIDs (e.g., naproxen, indomethacin) and steroids block the inflammatory products themselves. All three treat the acute attack only — uric acid does not change.

Allopurinol is a hypoxanthine look-alike. Xanthine oxidase converts it to oxypurinol, which stays tightly bound to the enzyme. In the double-reciprocal (Lineweaver-Burk) plot the inhibited line is steeper but meets the y-axis at the same point: same Vmax (top speed), higher Km (more substrate needed) — the pattern of a competitive inhibitor. The hypoxanthine that builds up can be salvaged or excreted.

URAT1 sits on the urine side (apical membrane) of proximal tubule cells. It reabsorbs urate from the tubular fluid while sending an organic anion such as lactate out. Probenecid and the other listed drugs block it, so more urate stays in the urine. They act through the kidney, so they fail when kidney function is poor. High lactate speeds the exchange, which is why alcohol and lactic acidosis raise urate.

Answer: C. An acute attack needs an anti-inflammatory drug. Naproxen (an NSAID) is the trap: NSAIDs worsen gastric ulcers. Probenecid, allopurinol and febuxostat lower uric acid over weeks and do not stop an acute flare.

One pathway, three diseases. ADA deficiency blocks adenosine → inosine [1] → ADA-SCID (severe combined immunodeficiency: no T, B or NK (natural killer) cells). PNP deficiency blocks inosine → hypoxanthine and guanosine → guanine [3] → T-cell deficiency only. Gout = too much end product, uric acid. Other steps: [2] 5′-nucleotidase, [4] guanase, [5] xanthine oxidase. The top (PRPP → IMP) is de novo synthesis feeding in. BMT = bone marrow transplant; ERT = enzyme replacement therapy.

γc (common gamma chain) is a shared part of the receptors for several interleukins (immune growth signals). Without it, T and NK cells don't develop, and B cells are present but useless without T-cell help. Don't confuse: X-SCID (X-linked) = T⁻ B⁺ NK⁻; ADA-SCID (autosomal recessive) = T⁻ B⁻ NK⁻, because dATP (deoxyadenosine triphosphate) poisons all lymphocytes.

Correction: the counts are per µL (microliter), not per mL. dATP shuts off ribonucleotide reductase, the only enzyme that makes deoxyribonucleotides (dNTPs, the DNA building blocks) from ribonucleotides. With no dNTPs, lymphocytes can't copy DNA or multiply, so both T cells (cell-mediated immunity) and B cells (antibodies, humoral immunity) fail.

Correction: PNP splits a nucleoside (inosine, guanosine), not a nucleotide. Phosphorolysis = breaking a bond with inorganic phosphate instead of water, which releases ribose 1-phosphate. Without PNP, deoxyguanosine builds up and becomes dGTP (deoxyguanosine triphosphate), which is toxic mainly to T cells. Fewer purine bases reach xanthine oxidase, so uric acid is low.

Answer: C. Low T, B and NK cells with low IgG = ADA-SCID, and ADA converts adenosine → inosine. E is the trap: ribonucleotide reductase is what dATP inhibits, not the defective enzyme. PNP deficiency would spare B cells and antibodies.

Unlike the purine ring, the pyrimidine ring is opened, so the end products are water-soluble (no crystal disease). Steps: nucleotide → nucleoside (nucleotidase) → free base (phosphorylase) → ring opened. Cytidine is first deaminated to uridine, so cytosine follows uracil → β-alanine → malonyl CoA (→ acetyl CoA, so "ketogenic"). Thymine → β-aminoisobutyrate → methylmalonyl CoA → succinyl CoA (a citric acid cycle intermediate, so "glucogenic").

Hereditary orotic aciduria: UMP synthase (UMP = uridine monophosphate; the enzyme turns orotic acid into UMP) is defective. Orotic acid spills into the urine and cells run short of pyrimidines → megaloblastic anemia that does not respond to vitamin B12 or folate, plus growth retardation. Treatment: uridine, which is salvaged to UMP. Don't confuse with OTC (ornithine transcarbamylase) deficiency of the urea cycle: orotic aciduria too, but with high ammonia and no anemia.

Diego and Jose are the same patient. Callos (tripe) and lengua (tongue) are organ meats; with red meat, they are among the richest sources of purines. Beer adds purines and alcohol. A sudden hot, swollen big-toe joint (first MTP, metatarsophalangeal, joint) is called podagra, the classic gout attack.

His BMI (body mass index = weight in kg ÷ height in m²) is 86 kg ÷ (1.80 m)² ≈ 26.5, overweight. Gout risk factors here: male sex, beer, extra weight, and a family history of diabetes, high blood pressure and high cholesterol (the metabolic syndrome cluster, which goes with high uric acid).

Abnormal: uric acid 12 (high); creatinine 2.0 and BUN (blood urea nitrogen) 25 (both high, so the kidneys filter poorly); lactic acid 20 (slightly high); WBC 12,000 (mild rise from inflammation). Glucose, lipids and calcium are normal.

Correction: the synovial WBC count is 20,000 per µL (microliter), not per mL. Urine pH 5.0 is acidic. In acid urine, urate takes its uncharged uric acid form, which dissolves poorly, so acid urine favors uric acid stones, the kind that fits his past kidney stones. The synovial findings are explained under question 1d.

PRPP (5-phosphoribosyl-1-pyrophosphate) is activated ribose 5-phosphate. The ring is built on it: glutamine gives the first amino group (the committed step), then glycine, aspartate, glutamine and THF (tetrahydrofolate, the folate form that carries one-carbon units) add the rest → IMP (inosine monophosphate; its base is hypoxanthine). IMP → GMP uses ATP and IMP → AMP uses GTP, which keeps the two balanced.

Drug targets: hydroxyurea blocks ribonucleotide reductase, which makes the deoxy (d) nucleotides used in DNA. 5-Fluorouracil blocks thymidylate synthase (dUMP → dTMP, the thymine nucleotide). Methotrexate, trimethoprim and pyrimethamine block DHFR (dihydrofolate reductase), which turns DHF (dihydrofolate) back into THF; without THF, no dTMP is made. Pyrimidines break down to soluble products, never uric acid.

CAD is one cytosolic protein carrying the first three enzymes (red boxes): CPS II (carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II), ATCase (aspartate transcarbamoylase) and dihydroorotase. UMP synthase carries the last two steps and makes UMP (uridine monophosphate). Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase is the only mitochondrial step.

Breakdown goes in three moves: nucleotidases remove the phosphate, nucleoside phosphorylase removes the ribose (as ribose 1-phosphate), then the base is oxidized. Adenine loses its amino group first (AMP → IMP or adenosine → inosine), so it ends as hypoxanthine. Guanine loses NH₄⁺ to become xanthine. Xanthine oxidase does hypoxanthine → xanthine → urate. Normally about 90% of freed hypoxanthine and guanine is salvaged back to nucleotides; only about 10% becomes uric acid.

Left chain, Lesch-Nyhan: without HGPRT (hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase, the salvage enzyme), hypoxanthine and guanine can't be recycled. Unused PRPP piles up and activates the amidotransferase, while IMP and GMP fall, so there is less inhibition. De novo synthesis speeds up, and the extra purines are broken down → high uric acid. HGPRT also turns allopurinol and 6-mercaptopurine into the nucleotides that block this step.

One clue settles each item. Trauma: a history of injury. Osteoarthritis: wear and tear, with no hot joint or fever. Rheumatoid arthritis: symmetric small joints of both hands, with morning stiffness. Septic arthritis: bacteria on Gram stain or culture of joint fluid (the dangerous one to rule out). Gout vs pseudogout: crystal shape in joint fluid. A hot big toe after a meat-and-beer feast points to gout.

Diego has both causes. Overproduction: organ meats and red meat are rich in nucleic acids, whose purines become uric acid, and beer adds more purines. Underexcretion: his kidneys filter poorly, and alcohol raises lactate. Why lactate: breaking down alcohol turns NAD⁺ into NADH (its reduced form). Excess NADH pushes lactate dehydrogenase to turn pyruvate into lactate, and lactate makes the kidney keep urate (question 4).

Creatinine and urea are wastes cleared mainly by filtration, so when GFR (glomerular filtration rate, the plasma volume the kidneys filter per minute) falls, both build up in blood. eGFR (estimated GFR) is calculated from serum creatinine, age and sex; “per 1.73 m²” scales it to an average adult body size. His 36 is moderate chronic kidney disease (yellow zone). The kidney excretes most uric acid, so he retains it.

20,000 WBC/µL, mostly neutrophils, means inflammatory fluid (normal is under 200; infection is usually over 50,000). Negative Gram stain and culture mean no bacteria, so not septic arthritis. Needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent crystals (yellow when parallel to the compensator axis) are MSU (monosodium urate), so this is gout. Pseudogout crystals (calcium pyrophosphate) are rhomboid and weakly positive (blue when parallel).

Follow steps 1–5. Macrophages in the joint take up MSU crystals and switch on the gene for pro-IL-1β, which they activate and release as IL-1β (interleukin-1 beta, an inflammation signal). IL-1β calls neutrophils out of nearby vessels into the joint, and they release more inflammatory chemicals, so the joint becomes hot, red, swollen and painful. IL-1β also causes his fever and high blood WBC. Colchicine works at step 4 by stopping neutrophil migration.

Answer: tophi, lumps of MSU crystals walled off by inflammatory tissue. They form after years of high uric acid. Blood urate normally sits close to its saturation point, so at 12 mg/dL body fluids are supersaturated and crystals precipitate. Urate dissolves less as temperature falls, so cool spots (big toe, fingers, elbow, ear) collect crystals first. Tophi mean chronic gout.

Xanthomas are cholesterol-filled lumps in skin or tendons, seen with very high LDL (e.g., familial hypercholesterolemia). Diego's lipids are normal (total cholesterol 170, LDL 90), which argues against xanthoma. Xanthelasmas are yellow cholesterol plaques on the eyelids. Fluid drawn from a tophus shows urate crystals, which settles it.

Answer to question 3: Years of high uric acid, from weak kidney excretion (eGFR 36) plus a purine-rich, beer-heavy diet, left urate crystals in cool joints (tophi) and in the kidney (stones). The feast pushed uric acid and lactate higher. New crystals formed in the joints, and the neutrophil inflammation they set off caused the acute flare, with fever and a high WBC. Crystals seen in joint fluid confirm gout. HPI = history of present illness; PTC = prior to consultation; IP jt = interphalangeal joint; N = normal.

Proximal tubule cell. On the urine side (apical membrane), URAT1 (urate transporter 1) takes urate back from the tubular fluid while sending an organic anion such as lactate out. GLUT9 (glucose transporter 9) on the blood side releases the urate into blood. More lactate in the cells drives more exchange, so more urate is reabsorbed and less is excreted. The listed drugs block URAT1 (uricosurics) but suit Diego poorly: they need good kidney function and raise the risk of uric acid stones.

His weak kidneys (eGFR 36) shape the choices. NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) block the prostaglandins that keep the afferent arteriole open, so they lower GFR further. Colchicine is cleared by the kidney, so it builds up and needs a lower dose. These drugs calm the flare but don't lower uric acid. Start allopurinol or febuxostat only after the flare settles (wait at least 2 weeks), because a sudden drop in urate can trigger new flares. Goal: urate below 6 mg/dL.

Uricase (urate oxidase) opens the purine ring of uric acid to make allantoin, which dissolves easily and is excreted. Humans lack a working uricase, so uric acid is our end product. Pegloticase is uricase given IV (into a vein). Its attached PEG (polyethylene glycol) chains make it less likely to trigger antibodies and keep it in blood longer. Allopurinol and febuxostat instead leave hypoxanthine and xanthine, which are more soluble than uric acid.

Why each step helps: less meat, organ meat, seafood and alcohol means fewer purines to break down and less lactate blocking urate excretion. Water dilutes the urine and lowers stone risk. Fructose is phosphorylated fast, using up ATP, and the extra AMP is broken down to uric acid.
